newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Capital-hungry Ansett sets 10 pct profit margin.
newsitem.headline: Capital-hungry Ansett sets 10 pct profit margin.

text.p: Loss-making Australian airline Ansett said on Sunday it was hungry for fresh capital and must achieve profit margins of about 10 percent to ensure its long-term viability.

Ansett executive chairman Rod Eddington said the airline would need a capital injection from its owners, media group News Corp and Air New Zealand, to fund a badly needed upgrade of its inefficient fleet.
But he said the two equal shareholders first needed to be persuaded that the fresh investment would deliver a sensible return and be convinced Ansett was flying toward profits.
"So I would be shooting for a target of about 10 percent profit as a percentage of sales," Eddington told the Nine Network's Business Sunday programme.
"Ansett needs more capital and in order to get it, it must fix its operating costs...and generate cash flows," he added.
"If it can do that, it will help its capital base and also encourage the two shareholders to step up to future capital injection."

Eddington, who ran Cathay Pacific Airways before taking over the controls at Ansett in January, says profits are "thin on the ground" despite the airline's domestic operation posting a small profit in the third quarter ended March 31.
Ansett's fledgling international service continued to operate at a loss in the quarter, according to News Corp's latest accounts.
"I believe both shareholders will invest capital provided they see themselves getting a sensible long-term return," Eddington said.

Ansett has begun work on a plan to achieve 10 percent profit margins, with the emphasis on cutting costs, selling non-core assets like tourism resorts and finding efficiencies through its partnership with Air New Zealand, he added.
Ansett and Air New Zealand want to merge some parts of their business, like maintenance and information and technology.
Ansett is shopping for eight new planes, at an estimated cost of around A$2 billion, in order to streamline its fleet to five different aircraft types from seven.
The contract is a close contest between European aircraft consortium Airbus Industrie's Airbus A330-200 and Boeing Co's 767-300.
Eddington said he would soon recommend his long-term fleet plan to Ansett's board. But, he added: "we can't rush this."
